exercises.name: Chin Tucks
exercises.form_cue: Keep doing them daily as a gym warm-up even though the dedicated session is now 2×/week. Chin back, hold 5 sec.
exercises.why: Maintenance dose. Your neck is strong now — this keeps the decompression habit and protects you as the bar gets heavy.

exercises.name: Multi-Direction Isometrics
exercises.form_cue: Resist your own hand in all four directions — flexion, extension, and each side. Hold 8 sec each. Firm but controlled.
exercises.why: Builds all-around cervical strength so the neck stabilises confidently under squats, deadlifts and your first overhead work.

exercises.name: Band Pull-Aparts
exercises.form_cue: Pull a band apart at chest height, squeeze the blades, relax the neck. Add a slightly stronger band.
exercises.why: Keeps the postural upper back strong and resilient as your pressing volume climbs.

exercises.name: Heavy-Slow Wrist Extension
exercises.form_cue: Heavier dumbbell now. Up over 3 sec, down over 3 sec. Mild tendon discomfort that settles quickly is fine; sharp pain is not.
exercises.why: Continued progressive loading fully restores tendon capacity so the elbow tolerates carries, rows and curls without flaring.

exercises.name: Hammer Curls
exercises.form_cue: Neutral grip (thumbs up), curl smoothly, control the lower. Neutral grip is the most elbow-friendly curl.
exercises.why: Strengthens the brachioradialis that crosses the elbow, sharing load away from the irritated extensor tendon.

exercises.name: Reverse Curls
exercises.form_cue: Palms down, light bar or dumbbells, curl up and control down. Stop short of any lateral elbow pain.
exercises.why: Directly loads the wrist extensors at longer muscle lengths — the final step in returning the tennis-elbow tendon to full strength.

exercises.name: Front Squat (or Back Squat)
exercises.form_cue: Bar on the front of the shoulders, elbows high, torso tall. Brace and sit between your hips. Eyes forward — never look up under load. Back squat is fine if the front rack bothers your wrists.
exercises.why: The front-rack position forces an upright torso and neutral neck, making it the most cervical-friendly way to squat heavy.

exercises.name: Trap-Bar or Conventional Deadlift
exercises.form_cue: Brace hard, neutral spine from head to hips, push the floor away. Keep the chin slightly tucked — resist the urge to look up. Use straps to protect the elbow.
exercises.why: Heavy hinging builds whole-body strength. With a neutral neck and braced trunk it's safe and powerfully protective for your back.

exercises.name: Barbell or DB Bench Press
exercises.form_cue: Shoulder blades pinned back and down, feet planted, head resting on the bench. Press in a slight arc. Don't push your head into the bench.
exercises.why: Builds horizontal pressing strength. The benched, supported position keeps the cervical spine quiet under heavier loads.

exercises.name: Seated DB Shoulder Press
exercises.form_cue: Upright bench with back support. Press dumbbells overhead, stopping just short of locking your neck back. INTRODUCE this cautiously — if any tingling or neck pain returns, drop back to the landmine press.
exercises.why: Your first true overhead work. Now that the neck has handled months of loading symptom-free, vertical pressing is reintroduced seated and controlled — the safest possible on-ramp.

exercises.name: Lat Pulldown / Weighted Row
exercises.form_cue: Pull to the upper chest, drive the elbows down, squeeze the lats. Keep the neck long — don't crane forward to chase the bar.
exercises.why: Heavy vertical and horizontal pulling balances all your pressing and keeps the upper back strong enough to hold good posture.

exercises.name: Loaded Walking Lunge
exercises.form_cue: Dumbbells at your sides, step into a lunge, drop the back knee, drive up. 10 steps per leg. Tall, braced torso.
exercises.why: Loaded single-leg strength and stability — directly transferable to powerful, injury-resistant running.

exercises.name: Suitcase Carry
exercises.form_cue: Hold one heavy dumbbell at your side, walk 40 sec tall and braced without leaning. Switch sides. Watch the grip on your elbow side.
exercises.why: Builds anti-lateral-flexion core and grip strength while teaching your trunk to stay rigid — superb, low-risk strength carryover.
